title: Quantum-Error-Correction, what? why? how? Explained by Google
bodyHtml:
Backstory:
The United Nations General Assembly announced 2025 to be the International Year of Quantum Science & Technology to mark 100 years since the development of quantum mechanics! It also marks a year since I got into quantum computing which I will celebrate by taking an oath of reading and decoding the latest quantum papers every month and writing about my understandings as standerdised blogs!

Paper: Suppressing quantum errors by scaling a surface code logical qubit by Google Quantum AI

Classical Reference: Quantum Error Correction (QEC)

The error-detection methods used in data transmission for classical computing inspired the QEC field because quantum computers are like analog computers and being analog means they will face physical hinderances (noise) while working.

No-cloning theorem which we covered in my Jan blog series, plays a crucial part in shaping the QEC field because unlike classical bits which we can duplicate/copy, qubits can’t be copied which makes many of our classical ways inapplicable in the quantum realm. The reasoning and detailed explanation can be found in my blogs or online.

Having said that, we have essentially established the foundation from which the QEC field stems from, now to understand more and dive deeper we will take a look at the first, simplest method that we can intuitively understand: Repetition Codes.

The repetition codes work on the logic that even if we cannot copy a qubit we can apply some gates on multiple qubits which work like copies and so it begins by encoding a logical qubit into n physical qubits. For example, if a logical qubit ∣0⟩ is encoded in 3 physical qubits, it is stored as ∣000⟩. Similarly, the logical state ∣1⟩ would be encoded as ∣111⟩. In a quantum computation, each physical qubit in the repetition code could potentially be affected by noise. If one of the qubits flips (say a ∣0⟩ flips to a ∣1⟩ or vice versa), the error can be detected by measuring the state of the qubits. Since the states are repeated across multiple qubits, the majority state (most common state) across all qubits gives the correct information. For instance, if ∣001⟩ is measured, the majority vote is 0, and the system infers that the qubit flip occurred in the second qubit. Once an error is detected (e.g., a flip in one of the qubits), the system can correct the state by flipping the incorrect qubit back to match the majority state. If there’s a single qubit error in the encoding (e.g., ∣010⟩), the system will know which qubit is incorrect and flip it back to the correct value.

Obviously, by these 2-bit-flips errors can’t be detected or corrected however, this is just the start, and building upon this core concept of repetition increases fault tolerance against noise. In this repetition code, we have 2 flavors: bit-flip & phase-flip error correctors which work independently and need to be combined to be useful for quantum computers, right? That’s where Shor Code comes in, however, I can’t go into it a lot because that’s not our objective in this blog however, I have created a presentation that explains basic QEC codes and also this paper in a quick bullet point method. Please email me to get the documents with the subject: “Medium QEC Blog: PPT”.

Introduction to Surface Codes

So, Shor Code was the first useful quantum error-correcting code that could detect both bit-flip and phase-flip errors. Further developments lead us to the popular code used in modern quantum computing: Surface Code.

In a surface code, the qubits are arranged in a 2D grid. Imagine a checkerboard pattern, where you have two types of spaces: some squares are used for storing the actual information (these are called data qubits), and other squares are used to check if anything went wrong (these are called ancilla qubits). The data qubits represent the logical quantum bits (or logical qubits), and the ancilla qubits help detect and fix errors.

Now, let’s break it down with a simple example. Imagine you’re encoding a qubit into a grid of 5 rows and 5 columns (a 5x5 grid). The data qubits, which hold your important information, are placed in certain spots in the middle of the grid. The rest of the qubits around them are ancilla qubits, whose job is to check for errors.

Here’s the cool part: If one of the data qubits gets messed up (for example, if it flips from 0 to 1 or 1 to 0), the ancilla qubits can detect this error by looking at their neighbors. This detection process is called syndrome measurement, and it tells you exactly where the error happened. Once the error is detected, you can correct it by flipping the wrong qubit back to its correct value.

If you notice properly, like an algorithm there are very simple steps at play in every type of QEC code which you should know to create your code if you want. The first is error detection mainly divided into 2 categories bit-flips and phase-flips, then once you know there is an error you want to locate the error which makes use of geometry and linear algebra for complex codes. Once you know the location of the error, you need to correct it which is by knowing the right answer, this step is flexible for different methods used in QEC so, here you can berserk!

The Experiment: Distance-3 vs Distance-5 Surface Codes

The term distance-x in a surface code indicates its error correction strength. A distance-x surface code can correct up to (x-1)/2 errors using 2x²-1 physical qubits. The higher the value of “x,” the more robust the error correction is, but it also requires more physical qubits.

Distance-3 uses 17 qubits: 9(3x3) data qubits & 8 measure qubits and corrects 1 error (bit/phase).
Distance-5 uses 49 qubits: 25(5x5) data qubits & 24 measure qubits and corrects 2 errors (bit/phase).

The experiment was conducted very cleverly because they used Google’s Sycamore 72-qubit quantum computer, where they used 49 physical qubits instead of 66 (49+17) needed for distance-3 & distance-5 surface codes by overlapping them to avoid any anomalies in individual qubits.

The blue part is the distance-5 surface code with the red border covering distance-3 surface code. They performed the same experiment multiple times which is a common scientific standard to avoid errors however, because the distance-3 surface code was utilizing the top corner, they also repeated the experiment by rotating the distance-3 surface code around the distance-5 grid. The circuit looked something like this:

The intricacies of the circuit aren’t covered in this blog because it is simply the implementation of surface code. However, as you can observe a series of Hadamard gates and Z/CZ gates are used which deal with phase-flip errors. Though doesn’t it seem off that we can detect and fix phase-flip errors in our last discussion, we concluded that it is through measurement that we can fix errors but phase collapses after measurement so, how? That’s because of stabilizers.

There are several types of stabilizers like weight-2 & weight-4 used in this experiment. The experiment was run for 25 cycles (50,000 experiment instances) and the analysis resulted in a 12% and 8% rise for distance-5, and distance-3 surface codes respectively. The relative consistency between code distances suggests that growing the lattice does not substantially increase the component error rates during error correction.

The Conclusion: Playing around Probabilities

The analysis after the results is the most fascinating part of the paper because they delve intensely into how they need to better their apparatus, or what were the errors and why they occurred. They also compare their experimental result to a simulated experiment they ran and so much more. The details are beyond me to put in this blog as they get extremely technical which if I present without explanation is no better than reading the paper itself however, I have summarized the pointers in my PPT about this paper which I will give you for free if you email me. The email instructions are mentioned above.

There is one thing that they cover at the end which is the most important part: scaling! Using so many qubits should be economical for their cost when multiplied by millions of logical qubits in a large-scale quantum computer. There is no clear answer to this however, this experiment is just the start, the main factor to consider when thinking about this topic is logical error per cycle and how increasing the distance can affect it. Here’s a graph that explains this trend:

As we can see in this graph that Google has only started to experiment with surface codes, and maybe in the future the trend will reveal better results with an increased number of code distance.

Personal Takeaways:

My thoughts on this subject are not in favor of surface codes and believe that there could be a better method that utilizes less number of physical qubits however, as a novice my ideas are a bit too good to be true. Because for now many researchers are trying to better surface code and I am talking about a whole new research into finding a new method that doesn’t rely on repetition as much. Instead of accepting that quantum computers are error-prone, I dream of creating a quantum computer that isn’t affected by noise as much as today or the way around. QEC for me is like overthinking this subject and working with what we have rather than investing time to create something a bit more powerful however, my approach isn’t industry-friendly at all and even though sounds good, has been tried out throughout the years.

This was my first attempt at reading a quantum-related paper by myself and trying to decode it into simpler terms, and I obviously don’t understand all of it however, by writing this blog I wanted a breakdown of the paper such that avid readers of quantum computing could be able to converse on this topic or find it interesting to read the paper themselves.
